summary: A UCLA Health news article dated March 8, 2023 reports that UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers identified how T cells 'see' and respond to mutations in cancer cells, which may explain why some patients respond to immunotherapy and others do not. The study, published in Nature, followed 11 patients with metastatic melanoma receiving anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy. The researchers suggest immune receptors from tumor-reactive T cells could be used to engineer T cells that target tumors even in non-responding patients.
one_line: UCLA researchers map how T cells recognize cancer mutations in melanoma patients on PD-1 immunotherapy, suggesting more personalized treatments.
key_facts: UCLA Health news article dated March 8, 2023, written by David Sampson, reports on a study of how immune cells 'see' and respond to cancer cells.
The study was led by scientists at the UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.
Cristina Puig-Saus, PhD, was the first author of the study published in Nature.
The study involved 11 patients with metastatic melanoma receiving anti-PD-1 'checkpoint inhibitor' immunotherapy.
Of the 11 patients, seven had a response to PD-1 blockade and four did not.
The number of mutations in the patients' tumors ranged between 3,507 and 31.
The number of mutations seen by tumor-reactive T cells ranged between 13 and one.
In patients with clinical benefit, the researchers isolated between 61 and seven different mutation-specific T cells in the blood and tumor.
In patients lacking a response, the researchers identified between 14 and two different T cells.
In responding patients, tumor-reactive T cells were detected in blood and tumors throughout treatment; in non-responders they were not recurrently detected.
Immune receptors from T cells of all patients, regardless of response, redirected immune cell specificity against the tumor, producing antitumor activity.
The new technique to isolate mutation-reactive T cells was built on technology developed with Antoni Ribas, James Heath, PhD, and David Baltimore, PhD.
The technology was further developed by PACT Pharma, using CRISPR gene editing to insert genes into immune cells.
The study's article is titled 'Neoantigen-targeted CD8+ T cell responses with PD-1 blockade therapy' with DOI 10.1038/s41586-023-05787-1.
